analysis.one_liner: Requires the President and Vice President to disclose and divest financial conflicts and release their tax returns.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 31 Senate Democrats, was referred to a Senate committee and never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President and Vice President to disclose their family's financial interests to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics, and to put any holding that could clash with their official duties into a blind trust whose trustee sells it off. It would require major-party presidential nominees and sitting presidents to make their last three years of tax returns public, bar presidential appointees from working on matters involving the president's own business, and extend the ban on members of Congress profiting from federal contracts to the President and Vice President. It also declares that violating these rules would count as an impeachable offense.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who wants to know whether the President is making decisions that enrich himself or his family. The bill would let the public see the president's tax returns, require conflicts to be sold off into blind trusts, and give state attorneys general and private citizens the ability to sue to enforce compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President and Vice President to disclose detailed financial interests of themselves, their spouses, and minor children to Congress and the Office of Government Ethics within 30 days of taking office, including for the officials already serving when the bill was written.

Requires divesting any financial interest that poses a potential conflict — including payments from foreign governments barred by the Constitution's emoluments clause — by transferring it to a qualified blind trust whose trustee must sell it and buy conflict-free holdings.

Requires the President and major-party presidential nominees to make their three most recent tax returns public, with the Office of Government Ethics and Federal Election Commission empowered to obtain them from the Treasury if they are not filed.

Bars presidential appointees from working on any matter involving the president's or the first spouse's own business interests, and extends the criminal ban on members of Congress holding lucrative federal contracts to the President and Vice President.

Allows the Attorney General, state attorneys general, or any aggrieved person to sue to enforce the divestiture rules, and states that a violation would constitute a high crime or misdemeanor under the Constitution's impeachment clause.

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, and their families, who would have to reveal their finances, sell off or blind-trust conflicting holdings, and release tax returns. An incumbent president with a large family business — the situation when this bill was written — would bear the largest burden.
analysis.who_pays_short: The President's family and business interests

drawbacks.text: Forcing a sitting President to sell off business assets could be challenged as intruding on executive power, and the bill itself concedes the point by including a severability clause in case parts are ruled unconstitutional.
Letting any 'aggrieved person' sue the President over divestiture could invite a stream of politically motivated lawsuits against every occupant of the office, not only the one the bill was aimed at.
Publicly releasing years of tax returns of candidates and their families raises privacy concerns for relatives who did not choose to run for office, even with redactions allowed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on one officeholder and one family at a time, while the benefit — being able to see whether the country's top elected official is personally profiting from his decisions — applies to everyone. The main design risks are legal vulnerability and the possibility of harassment suits, but the core requirements mirror rules already applied to other federal officials.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate committee that handles government ethics and sat there for the rest of the Congress without ever getting a hearing, a vote, or a floor debate.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill in the Senate on March 26, 2019, joined by 30 Democratic cosponsors — every one of them a Democrat, with no Republican support.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which handles government ethics matters.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever taken on the bill.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The sitting President and his family business were better off, since no divestiture, tax-return release, or recusal requirement ever took effect. Incumbents generally benefit, because presidents and their families remain exempt from the financial-conflict rules that apply to other federal employees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The incumbent President and his family business

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Presidential Conflicts of Interest Act of 2019 and organized its Senate support.

for.name: 30 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Klobuchar, Booker, Harris, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 30 were Democrats and no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Sen. Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: As the sitting President whose finances the bill would have covered, he had refused to release his tax returns and did not support the bill; his party controlled the Senate committee where it stalled.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no action in the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred.

industries.industry: Presidential family business holdings (e.g., large real-estate and hotel empires)
industries.note: The bill would force the President's family to divest any holding that conflicts with official duties, including interests in entities owned or controlled by foreign governments. An incumbent with a large family business would have to sell or blind-trust it, which is the situation the bill was written for.

Payments from foreign states or their owned entities to the President are treated as potential conflicts the bill requires divesting, closing a channel through which foreign governments could seek favor with the administration.

industries.industry: Government contractors and officeholders seeking federal contracts
industries.note: The bill extends the existing criminal ban on Members of Congress profiting from federal contracts to the President and Vice President, closing the same loophole for the executive branch that already applies to legislators.
